newsitem.title: UK: Plasma trade can spread HIV, researchers say.
newsitem.headline: Plasma trade can spread HIV, researchers say.

text.p: A rapid rise in cases of AIDS among heterosexuals in the Third World may be due to HIV infection among paid donors of blood plasma, researchers said on Friday.
People who donate blood plasma can catch HIV, the infection that causes AIDS, from contaminated equipment and then transmit it to recipients of future donations.

In a letter to the Lancet medical journal, Dr Patricia Volkow and colleagues working in Mexico described the cases of two families in which several members who were paid donors of plasma, the liquid part of blood, later died of AIDS.

Plasma donation involves taking blood and then reinjecting the cells from the blood back into the donor. Contamination of the equipment, often by reusing items which should only be used once and then disposed of, can lead to HIV infection.

The researchers said "improper" plasma extraction techniques using contaminated equipment had led to HIV infection among paid donors, who had then infected recipients of their blood and plasma products, and their own sexual partners.
They said that by July 1996, 357 AIDS cases had been reported among paid plasma donors in Mexico, twice the number of AIDS cases among haemophiliacs.

"We want to alert the international community to an efficient way of spreading HIV which has been largely ignored in most explanations of the rapid increase of HIV and AIDS in heterosexual populations in developing countries," the researchers said.

They said paid donors represented an important source of blood in many developing countries and were also a source of plasma exported to developed countries. It was often not possible to identify the country of origin of imported plasma.
"We urge colleagues...to take a hard look at blood and the contribution of the plasma trades to the HIV epidemic internationally and especially in the developing world," the researchers said.
